$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) &=a(t){x}_{1}(t)+b(t){x}_{2}(t)+f(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) &=c(t){x}_{1}(t)+d(t){x}_{2}(t)+g(t)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where

- $a(t),$ $b(t),$ $c(t),$ $d(t),$ $f(t),$ and $g(t)$ are known functions, and

- $x_1(t)$ and $x_2(t)$ are unknown functions (dependent variables). 
Such a system can always be written in the form

$$
\mathbf x'(t) = A\mathbf x(t) + \mathbf f(t)
$$

where

$$
\mathbf x(t) = 
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{bmatrix},
\quad
A = 
\begin{bmatrix}a(t) & b(t) \\ c(t) & d(t)\end{bmatrix},
\quad
\mathbf f(t) = 
\begin{bmatrix}f(t) \\ g(t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We have the following system.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)+3{x}_{1}(t)-4{x}_{2}(t) &=0 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)-\sqrt{2}{x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t) &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Writing our system in standard form, we get the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) &=-3{x}_{1}(t)+4{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) &=\sqrt{2}{x}_{1}(t)-2{x}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we can rewrite our system in matrix form as follows:

$$
\mathbf x'(t) = 
\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 4 \\ \sqrt{2} & -2\end{bmatrix} \mathbf x(t)
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
A=
	\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 4 \\ \sqrt{2} & -2\end{bmatrix}.

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the predators and $y=y(t)$ represents the prey.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=-0.4x+0.4xy \\ {y}^{′} &=y-4xy\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Evaluate the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium point $\mathbf{x^\ast}=[0.25, \, 1]^T,$ and classify this equilibrium point.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let's denote $f_1(x,y)=-0.4x+0.4xy$ and $f_2(x,y)=y-4xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-0.4x+0.4xy)=-0.4+0.4y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-0.4x+0.4xy)=0.4x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y-4xy)=-4y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y-4xy)=1-4x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is
$$
J
=
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}- 0.4 + 0.4 y & 0.4 x \\ - 4 y & 1 - 4 x\end{array} \right]}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium $\mathbf{x}^\ast = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}0.25 \\ 1\end{array} \right]}$ to get

$$
J(\mathbf{x}^\ast)
=
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}- 0.4 + 0.4 ( 1 ) & 0.4 ( 0.25 ) \\ - 4 ( 1 ) & 1 - 4 ( 0.25 )\end{array} \right]}
=
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}\bbox[4pt,border:1pt solid gainsboro]{0} & \bbox[4pt,border:1pt solid gainsboro]{0.1} \\ \bbox[4pt,border:1pt solid gainsboro]{- 4} & \bbox[4pt,border:1pt solid gainsboro]{0}\end{array} \right]}.
$$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}-\lambda  & 0.1 \\ -4 & -\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-\lambda )(-\lambda )-(-4)\cdot 0.1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+0.4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues $\lambda_{1,2} = \pm 0.2\sqrt{10}\,\text{i}.$ Since the eigenvalues are purely imaginary, our equilibrium is a stable center.

**Note:**
For the Lotka-Volterra model (as in this problem), it is safe to classify the nonzero equilibrium as a center when the linearization has purely imaginary eigenvalues. 

**Watch out!** 
In contrast, for a general nonlinear system, the Jacobian test alone is inconclusive (additional analysis is required to determine whether the equilibrium is a true center or a spiral sink/source).

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -3 & 4\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 0 \\ -3{\alpha }_{1}t & 4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

where $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda) = \alpha_1 \lambda + \alpha_0.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
\lambda_1=t, \qquad
\lambda_2=4t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(t) &={e}^{t} \\ r(4t) &={e}^{4t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{t} \\ 4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{4t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0{:}$

- Subtracting the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
3t\alpha_1 = e^{4t} - e^{t}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\alpha_1 = \dfrac{1}{3t}\bigl(e^{4t}-e^{t}\bigr).
$$

- Multiplying the first equation by $4$ and subtracting the second one, we get

$$
3\alpha_0 = 4e^{t} - e^{4t}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\alpha_0 = \dfrac{1}{3}\bigl(4e^{t}-e^{4t}\bigr).
$$

Substituting $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ into the expressions for the entries of $e^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\left(\frac{1}{3t}({e}^{4t}-{e}^{t})\right)t+\frac{1}{3}(4{e}^{t}-{e}^{4t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}({e}^{4t}-{e}^{t}+4{e}^{t}-{e}^{4t}) \\  & ={e}^{t} \\ -3{\alpha }_{1}t & =-3\left(\frac{1}{3t}({e}^{4t}-{e}^{t})\right)t \\  & ={e}^{t}-{e}^{4t} \\ 4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =4\left(\frac{1}{3t}({e}^{4t}-{e}^{t})\right)t+\frac{1}{3}(4{e}^{t}-{e}^{4t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}((4{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{t})+(4{e}^{t}-{e}^{4t})) \\  & ={e}^{4t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,
$$
e^{At} = 
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{e}^{t} & 0 \\ {e}^{t} - {e}^{4 t} & {e}^{4 t}\end{array} \right]}.
$$

$$

$$

=
